Eshwar Mahenthiralingam, Adam Baldwin, Pavel Drevinek, and co-authors put an old typing tool to a new use in 2006. Multilocus sequence typing identifies microbes by reading a set of their housekeeping genes. A metagenome, by contrast, is all the DNA scooped from an environment at once, a mix from many species, most never grown in a lab.

The authors showed that sequence typing could pull order out of that mix, naming the strains hiding in the metagenome. Their title says the method breathes life into the data: raw sequences become known organisms with known traits. That matters wherever microbes matter, from soil and water to the bacteria that infect vulnerable patients.

Prime Minister Churchill sent President Roosevelt telegram number 504 from London on 13 November 1943, a personal and most-secret protest about French actions in Syria and Lebanon. French forces had seized the Lebanese president and ministers, and Churchill calls the acts lamentable outrages.

He argues the arrests mock the Atlantic Charter and show what de Gaulle's leadership of France means, warning of grave fallout across the Arab world. His proposed course is joint and hard: demand the prisoners be freed and the assembly restored. If de Gaulle refuses, the Allies should withdraw recognition from the French National Committee. They should also halt the arming of French troops in North Africa. He adds a warning that de Gaulle, with armed forces at hand, might do anything.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d317: President Roosevelt received a brief telegram from Secretary of State Cordell Hull, sent from Washington on 25 November 1943. It relays Lisbon's cable 2835 of 23 November, which announces that the group of American army and navy technicians had left Horta the day before for Terceira Island in the Azores. Hull adds that the early departure of these American technicians was thanks to British cooperation at Horta. The short message marks the American build-up on the Portuguese islands moving from negotiation to men on the ground.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d417:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent Secretary of State Hull an urgent telegram from Moscow on 6 December 1943. Numbered 2131, it explains what he knew of the Soviet announcement that had scooped the Tehran communiqué. Harriman had returned to Moscow only the night before.

The newspaper announcement of 4 December, he writes, was a complete surprise to him. The conference agreement was plain. The two declarations were to be released not before eight in the evening, Moscow time, on 6 December. Release was to be simultaneous in London, Moscow, and Washington. For security, no mention of the conference was to be made before that hour. He was present when that was understood. Molotov, newly back himself, has not yet been seen, so Harriman can offer no explanation yet, though he guesses the Reuters reports and Senator Connally's broadcast pushed Moscow to speak.

Lincoln MacVeagh, the American ambassador to the Greek government-in-exile in Egypt, wrote to Secretary of State Hull on December 12, 1943. The exiled Greek government worked from Cairo while German forces held Greece itself. The State Department printed MacVeagh's message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

MacVeagh reported on a government without a country, split by politics and shadowed by armed resistance movements at home. His messages helped Washington judge what Greece would need when liberation came. For readers, this report opens the Greek side of the Cairo story, where the questions were not invasions and fleets but legitimacy, relief, and who would rule after the Germans left.

Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, wrote to President Roosevelt on July 26, 1944. Hopkins lived at the White House and saw Roosevelt daily, so a written message from him usually marked a considered judgment. It appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Hopkins advised Roosevelt on everything from Russian relations to the management of allies, and his written words carried into the planning for the Quebec Conference that September. A Hopkins memorandum in the pre-conference file shows the President's inner circle preparing the ground. For readers, it is a glimpse of the advice Roosevelt trusted most, given by the man who knew his mind best.

The Polish ambassador had just visited him with an urgent appeal from Premier Mikołajczyk and Foreign Minister Romer. Attached is the Polish memorandum itself, dated September 4.

The appeal begged for food, arms, and medical supplies for the Home Army fighting in Warsaw. It reported the Old Town lost, munitions nearly gone, and food rationed only to September 7. A large British air operation had just been judged impossible. Bohlen noted Admiral Leahy had promised to raise the matter with the president and the Joint Chiefs.

arxiv-2606-07017: Foundation model agents trained in simulation stumble in reality — the sim-to-real gap. This paper unifies the gap under an MDP perspective for foundation model agents. The unified view points to principled fixes. MDPs frame the reality gap. Simulation is not the territory.
arxiv-2606-07117: Generating 3D scenes end-to-end — meshes plus textures, semantically aligned — is the goal. Native3D does it with unified mesh-texture modeling and semantic alignment. The unified approach generates coherent worlds.  Coherent 3D worlds emerge from unified generative models. Generation meets semantic understanding here.
arxiv-2606-07217: Robots adapting to new tasks can meta-learn in weight space — not just in behavior. This paper adapts robotic policies via weight-space meta-learning. The weight-space view makes adaptation fast and principled. Weight space offers fast adaptation. Meta-learning finds good starting points.
arxiv-2606-07317: Generative retrieval — models that generate document IDs — needs efficient attention. This gated bidirectional linear attention serves that need. The gating makes retrieval both fast and accurate. Generative retrieval must be fast and accurate. The gated attention delivers both qualities.
arxiv-2606-07417: Reaction-diffusion equations driven by rough non-trace-class noise need a local theory. This paper builds an optimal one. The theory handles the noise rigorously. Rough stochastic noise challenges PDE theory. The constructed local theory is provably optimal. Rigor prevails. This is a deep and technically demanding result.
tob-10017:
Job is the eighteenth book in this King James ordering, and its author is unknown. Its central figure is a righteous man who loses family, wealth, and health in a single sweep of disaster. The story is told largely as poetry, in long speeches rather than plain narrative.

Job's friends insist his suffering must be punishment for some sin. Job rejects that answer and demands to plead his case before God. God finally speaks from a whirlwind, answering with questions about creation rather than an explanation. Few ancient books press the problem of undeserved pain so openly, or leave the sufferer still speaking back.
tob-10817:
Israel Abrahams walked through the whole of Jewish literature in Chapters on Jewish Literature, in short, readable chapters. Bible and Talmud come first, then medieval philosophy and poetry, and finally modern writers. Three thousand years of writing pass through one slim volume, with each stop chosen to highlight essentials.

Abrahams explains what the essential books are and why they matter, rather than merely listing titles. His map helps readers place a name like Maimonides or a form like Midrash in a living sequence. For students beginning Jewish studies, or general readers filling a gap, Abrahams remains a humane guide who assumes curiosity, not prior knowledge.
tob-4017:
Vasari crowns his history in volume three with the giants: Leonardo, Raphael, and above all Michelangelo, whom he worshipped as art's culmination. The volume runs to Vasari's own contemporaries, making the ending read like a victory lap for his age and city. Florence, in his telling, has led art back to life and beyond the ancients.

Many famous Renaissance legends survive only because Vasari recorded them, which makes the volume source and suspect at once. His Michelangelo material draws on personal acquaintance and devotion. Students still start here for the stories behind the works, then check them against documents Vasari never saw or chose not to use.
tob-0117:
Organized Freemasonry dates its public life from James Anderson's Constitutions of 1723. The young Grand Lodge of England ordered the book, and Anderson, a Scottish minister, compiled it. Lodges across the world still treat it as their founding charter.

A legendary history runs from Adam through Solomon's temple to London, giving the craft an ancient pedigree. Then come the Charges, rules of conduct for Masons, and the Regulations for running lodges. Every later Masonic constitution descends from these pages. This entry draws on a checked pre-1930 edition. Few club rulebooks have ever mattered so much.
tob-4117:
Volume two of Bhishagratna's Sushruta Samhita turns from the operating room to the clinic. Sickness, fevers, and poisons fill its pages, with their causes, signs, and cures set out in the Ayurvedic manner. Bhishagratna finished the translation in 1911 from the Sanskrit.

Snakebite, madness, and diseases of eye and ear each get their regimen of herbs, oils, and diet. The physician's judgment matters as much as the drugs. Together the two volumes give Ayurveda's surgical classic in full English dress. Checked from the 1919 printing, book two completes a landmark: the Indian healer's handbook, whole at last.
fludd-utriusque-cosmi-vol-1-macrocosmi-1:
English physician Robert Fludd began his history of both worlds in 1617. This first tract treats the macrocosm, the great world outside man. Fludd defended Rosicrucian ideas in print against sharp critics.

He maps creation from God through stars, elements, and living kinds. Music, number, and light order his cosmos at every level. Engravings by famed artists made the set a visual landmark. The Latin text is dense and wholly confident. The volume opens a grand system in which heaven and earth mirror each other at every step. Few systems of the age reach so far.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-17:
Volume seventeen of Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud joins three tractates: Maccoth, Shebuoth, and Eduyoth. Maccoth treats false witnesses and the cities of refuge. Shebuoth is the tractate of oaths, and Eduyoth gathers testimonies that fix points of law.

Maccoth rules that lying witnesses suffer the fate they planned for their victim, and maps the refuge cities for a man who kills by accident. Shebuoth then sorts oaths: rash vows, oaths in court, and oaths that bind the future. Eduyoth closes the volume as a record of agreed rulings, kept so later courts could lean on them. The trio shows law guarding truth itself.
linnaean-society-gloucester-sea-serpent-:
Learned men of New England took sworn proof on a sea serpent in the summer of 1817. The Linnaean Society's report tells of a great marine animal seen near Cape Ann, off Gloucester, by scores of witnesses. A committee of the society was charged to take the facts down in form.

Witnesses swore to the beast's size, its humps, and its swift, smooth run through the bay. The committee prints their words and weighs them like a court of law. No earlier sea serpent case got so strict a hearing from men of science. The report set the bar for how such claims should be tried.
machen-terror-1917:
Nature itself turns on man in Machen's wartime mystery of 1917. The Terror tells of deaths on farms and roads that no human hand can own. Beasts band, strike, and vanish, and a hush of fear falls on the country.

Machen wrote with the Great War at full roar, and the dread of the hour fills his fields. His guess at the cause ties the revolt of the beasts to man's own fall from grace. The book is the weird tale of the war years at its most strong. It channels a whole age's fear into the hedgerows.
barrett-threshold-of-the-unseen-1917:
William Barrett sums up forty years of hunts in On the Threshold of the Unseen, his book of 1917. Barrett was a man of science who helped found the chief band for such study. He had sat in dark rooms, weighed frauds, and met claims of all kinds. Here he tells what he holds stands firm past all fair doubt.

Ghosts, thought leaps, and life past death get a calm, grave weigh. He backs faith, yet keeps a tester's care. The book is a life's work in one tome. It is the field's best short sum from a founder.
bogoras-koryak-texts-1917:
Waldemar Bogoras gathered these Koryak texts in the field in northeast Siberia, and the set came out in 1917. The Koryak are near kin to the Chukchi of the same coast. His work formed part of the Jesup work in the North Pacific.

Each text stands in the Koryak tongue with an English version set beside it. Bogoras took care to keep names, songs, and odd turns of speech just as he heard them. The tales and rite texts include shaman songs, myths, and speech used in rites. For those who study lost tongues and oral lore, the book keeps the Koryak voice on record.
woodward-piltdown-fourth-note-1917:
Arthur Smith Woodward, keeper at the British Museum, gave this fourth note on the Piltdown gravel in 1917. Grafton Elliot Smith adds a part on the brain cast of the find. Piltdown man was then held a true dawn man of England by its chief backers.

The note tells of a new find spot, with parts of a second skull of the same kind. That 'Piltdown II' skull seemed to prove the first was no freak or chance mix. In truth both were fraud, and the note shows the hoax at its most safe and sure hour.
balfour-declaration-1917:
Arthur James Balfour, the foreign secretary of Britain, sent this short letter on November 2, 1917. He sent it to Lord Rothschild, head of the great bank house. Balfour asked him to pass its words on to the Zionist Federation.

In one brief passage, Britain backs the plan for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. The letter adds that the rights of the folk now in that land must not be harmed by the plan. Few short letters have shaped the fate of a land as this one has since.
austen-persuasion-1817:
Jane Austen's Persuasion came out in 1817, after her death, her final full novel. Anne Elliot gets a quiet, autumnal second chance at love in its pages. At nineteen she broke her engagement to Wentworth on a friend's advice and pressure.

Eight years later, Wentworth returns, now a rich naval captain with fame. Anne watches him court others while her own bloom and spirits slowly revive. A fall at Lyme and a famed letter at Bath resolve the long strain. Austen writes with a mellow depth unique in her six great novels here. Many readers rank this tender book as her most moving work.
austen-northanger-abbey-1817:
Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey came out in 1817, after her death, a Gothic parody. Catherine Morland, a keen reader of Gothic novels, lets her fancy run wild. Austen wrote the book young, and its bounce shows her early comic gift at work.

Catherine visits Bath, makes friends, and falls for the witty Henry Tilney there. At his abbey home she hunts for horrid secrets that do not exist at all. A locked cabinet and a laundry list deflate her wildest dark dreams in Bath. She learns that real life has its own quiet wrongs to face bravely. Austen teases Gothic craze while she defends novels and their young readers.
millay-renascence-1917:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published Renascence and Other Poems in 1917, her debut collection, crowned by the title poem. The voice of the Jazz Age's new woman first speaks here, in lyrics of candor. Millay had written Renascence at nineteen, and its prize scandal of 1912 first carried her name to editors.

Renascence, a long lyric, rises from a grave's imagined depths to a soul's rebirth in rain and light. The other poems, sonnets and songs of love, death, and the sea, show her formal gift and her frankness. Thursday, The Dream, and Sorrow display the wit and ache that would make her a popular poet laureate of youth. Camden, Maine, and Vassar stand behind verse that New York bohemia would soon claim as its own. The book is a debut of rare completeness, its best poems still anthology fixtures.
hamsun-growth-of-soil-1917:
Knut Hamsun published Growth of the Soil in 1917, a novel about a man who builds a farm from wild land. Isak walks into the Norwegian wilderness and clears fields stone by stone. His wife Inger joins him, and a home, children, and livestock follow. Neighbors settle nearby, and a small community grows.

The story moves at the pace of seasons and hard labor. Against Isak's steady work, Hamsun sets greed, crime, and town values that pull others astray. The novel won wide fame and helped earn Hamsun the Nobel Prize. It remains a powerful praise of the land and of patient, simple work.
eliot-prufrock-1917:
T. S. Eliot published Prufrock and Other Observations in 1917, his first book of poems. The opening poem gives the love song of J. Alfred Prufrock, a timid man at a social gathering. Prufrock longs to speak and act but fears how others will judge him. Other poems sketch lonely rooms, streets, and women in London and Boston.

Eliot's lines mix high and low speech in a new, ironic music. Images of fog, evenings, and empty talk build a mood of drift. The book was small but its impact was large. It announced a break with the poetry of the past. Many see it as the moment modern poetry truly began.
adler-neurotic-constitution-1917:
Alfred Adler published The Neurotic Constitution in German in 1912. The English text here is the 1917 translation by Bernard Glueck and John E. Lind. Adler, a former colleague of Freud, founds here his individual psychology. The feeling of inferiority, he argues, drives people to strive and compensate.

Neurotics, in his account, set fictional goals of superiority they cannot reach. Their symptoms serve those goals as excuses and safeguards. Adler stresses social feeling and conscious purpose over Freud's drives. Organ inferiority and childhood experience shape the striving style. The book is the founding text of Adlerian therapy. Its ideas on inferiority entered common speech.
ricardo-principles-1817:
David Ricardo was a London stockbroker who retired rich and turned to writing on money, rent, and trade. His Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, published in 1817, is the engine room of classical economics. Later thinkers from Marx to modern trade theorists built on its frame.

Ricardo argues that rent rises as farming is pushed onto poorer land, while wages and profit pull against each other. His best-known idea, comparative advantage, shows how two nations both gain when each makes what it makes best. The reasoning is dry and tight, and it still drives debate on trade.
tagore-nationalism-1917:
In Nationalism, published in 1917, Tagore prints lectures he gave in Japan and America during the First World War. He warns his hearers that nationalism, the worship of the nation as a machine of power, is a spiritual menace. The warning sounded strange while empires were at war.

Tagore argues that the modern state, built for gain and force, crushes the social and moral life of a people. He speaks to Japan, to America, and to his own India in turn, urging each toward a wider human loyalty. His critique of the modern state still reads as prophecy to many.
coover-experiments-in-psychical-research:
John E Coover published Experiments in Psychical Research in 1917, reporting work done at Stanford University. Coover held a research post set up to test claims of telepathy and other psychic powers. His book was an early American attempt to test such claims inside a university lab.

Tests used cards, drawings, and word lists, with sender and receiver kept apart and results scored against chance. Coover found that his long runs of trials gave no clear proof of telepathy beyond what chance would predict. That sober result made the book a landmark: it set a high bar for later lab work on claimed psychic gifts.
mickiewicz-pan-tadeusz-noyes-1917:
George Rapall Noyes published his translation of Adam Mickiewicz's Pan Tadeusz in 1917, the first complete English version of Poland's national epic. Mickiewicz wrote the long poem in exile in Paris in 1834. It opens with a hymn to Lithuania, then part of the Russian Empire, as his lost homeland.

The poem follows a gentry feud, a love story, and secret hopes as Napoleon's army nears in 1812. Hunting feasts, mushroom gatherings, and court cases fill its verses with old Polish life. Noyes rendered the poem in English prose with full notes. For English readers, his version opened a classic that Poles learn by heart.
lenin-imperialism-1917:
Vladimir Lenin wrote Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism in 1916, and it appeared in 1917; this entry uses the Vanguard Press edition of 1926. Lenin wrote in exile in Zurich during the First World War. He sought the economic roots of that war in the growth of giant firms and banks.

Lenin argued that free competition had given way to monopoly, and that finance capital now ruled and divided the world among great powers. Colonies and spheres of influence, in his account, must be fought over again and again. The theory of imperialism as capitalism's highest stage shaped communist thought and anti-colonial movements across the twentieth century.
lenin-state-and-revolution-1917:
Vladimir Lenin wrote The State and Revolution in 1917, while in hiding in Finland. It appeared that year, and this entry uses the Vanguard Press edition of 1926. Lenin set out, from Marx and Engels, what should happen to the state after a workers' revolution.

The old state machine, he argued, must be smashed, not merely taken over, and replaced by a commune-like order of armed workers. That order, the dictatorship of the proletariat, would then wither away as class rule ended. Lenin left the book unfinished as the October Revolution began. It became the core text of his theory of the state and a lasting point of argument among Marxists.
bukharin-imperialism-world-economy-1917:
Nikolai Bukharin wrote Imperialism and World Economy in 1917, with an introduction by Lenin; this entry uses the International Publishers edition of 1929. Bukharin, a young Bolshevik theorist, built a companion work to Lenin's own study of imperialism. His focus was the economics beneath the politics.

Bukharin described how trusts and banks fuse into finance capital, and how state capitalist trusts then compete on a world scale. War, in his account, grows from that competition as surely as price wars grow among firms. Lenin prized the book and borrowed from its scheme. It remains a clear statement of the Marxist theory of imperialism's economics, written before its author rose and fell in Soviet politics.
byron-manfred-1817:
Lord Byron wrote Manfred in Switzerland during the stormy summer of 1816, the same season that produced Frankenstein. He called it a dramatic poem rather than a stage play. It was published in 1817 and quickly became one of his most famous works.

Manfred is a nobleman and magician living alone in the Alps, crushed by guilt over a lost beloved. He summons spirits and demands forgetfulness, but refuses to bow to any power, good or evil. Even at death he defies the demons who come for him. The poem is Byron's answer to Faust and the purest portrait of his defiant hero.
coleridge-biographia-literaria-1817:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge meant to write a short preface about his life and opinions. Instead the preface grew into Biographia Literaria, his sprawling book of autobiography and literary theory, published in 1817. All twenty-four chapters are included here.

Coleridge explains his famous split between imagination, which creates and unifies, and fancy, which only rearranges. He also gives a long, respectful argument with Wordsworth's views on poetic language. Mixed in are memories of his schooldays, his friendship with Wordsworth, and his opium struggles. The book founded much of modern literary criticism in English, flaws and all.
wharton-summer-1917:
Edith Wharton published Summer in 1917, setting it in a poor Berkshire village she called North Dormer. Wharton usually wrote about rich New Yorkers. Here she turned to a young woman with almost nothing, and produced her boldest novel of female desire.

Charity Royall, adopted from a lawless mountain settlement, works in the village library and suffocates under her guardian's eye. A young architect, Lucius Harney, arrives to study old houses, and a summer love affair follows. Charity's awakening brings freedom and danger in equal parts, ending in pregnancy and hard choices. Wharton treats her heroine's longing without a hint of shame. The book shocked readers who expected safer fare from her.
robinson-merlin-1917:
Edwin Arlington Robinson turned to the Arthurian legends for Merlin, a long blank-verse poem published in 1917. Robinson had spent two decades writing about small-town failures in Maine. Here he tested his powers on the grandest story material in English tradition.

Robinson's Merlin is no stage magician but a weary, self-aware man who foresees the ruin of Camelot. He leaves Arthur's court for love with Vivian, knowing the escape cannot last. Around them the fellowship of the Round Table rots from within. The poem treats the legend as a mirror for a world sliding toward war, which readers in 1917 felt keenly. Merlin is Robinson's most ambitious single poem.
sinclair-king-coal-1917:
Upton Sinclair published King Coal in 1917, drawing on the Colorado coal strike of 1913 and 1914 and the Ludlow Massacre that ended it. Sinclair had visited the strike zone, picketed in New York for the miners, and been arrested for his pains. The novel sends a rich man's son into the camps in disguise.

Hal Warner, a coal operator's heir, takes a job under a false name to learn the mines from inside. He finds company towns run like feudal estates: scrip pay, cheated weights, and guards against organizers. A mine disaster turns his education into action, and he joins the strike he came to observe. Sinclair builds his case like a prosecutor. King Coal is his novel of the mine wars, still the fullest fictional record of them.
williams-al-que-quiere-1917:
William Carlos Williams was a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey, who wrote poems between house calls. Al Que Quiere, published in 1917, is the book where his own voice first comes through clearly. Its Spanish title means roughly 'to him who wants it,' and the full title carries an exclamation point. The poems turn away from fancy European models toward plain American speech.

Williams writes about local people, streets, flowers, and small daily scenes around him. He favors short lines, sharp images, and the rhythms of talk he heard every day. Some pieces are tender, others wry or blunt. The book laid the ground for his lifelong project: a poetry built from American things, seen up close.
larochefoucauld-maxims-heard-1917:
François de La Rochefoucauld, a French duke who had fought and schemed at court, published his Maxims in 1665. John Heard Jr. translated the full set of 504 maxims into English in 1917. Each maxim is a sentence or two, honed until it cuts.

Again and again La Rochefoucauld finds self-love hiding behind fine motives. Friendship, pity, courage, and even virtue itself come under his cold gaze. Yet the tone is polished, not bitter, and many lines ring with rueful truth. Readers have mined the maxims for three centuries as a guide to human nature. They founded the French tradition of the moralist, the cool judge of manners and hearts.
chekhov-lady-with-dog-1917:
Constance Garnett's 1917 volume of Anton Chekhov's stories takes its name from The Lady with the Dog. In that tale a bored Moscow banker meets a young married woman at the seaside town of Yalta. Their casual flirtation deepens, against all plans, into the one real love of their lives.

The other stories in the volume show Chekhov's mature range in Garnett's smooth English. Clerks, landowners, doctors, and wives pass through brief scenes that reveal whole lives. Nothing is forced and little is resolved, yet every detail tells. The title story alone is often called the finest love story in Russian writing. The volume is a fine door into Chekhov.
chekhov-party-1917:
The Party and Other Stories reached English readers in 1917 in Constance Garnett's translation. The title story follows Olga Mihalovna through a name-day party at her country house. Smiling for guests all day, she hides a failing marriage and her own despair until the strain breaks through.

A Doctor's Visit, another strong piece in the volume, sends a young doctor to a factory owner's sick daughter. He finds the illness rooted in wealth, idleness, and a useless life. Chekhov builds such stories from talk, glances, and small acts rather than big events. These middle-period tales show his art at its calmest and most exact. Garnett's set made them standard reading in English.
machado-poesias-completas-1917:
Antonio Machado gathered his Poesías completas in 1917, and the text here is the Spanish original. No English translation of the complete poems is in the public domain. The volume holds Soledades, his early book of inward, garden-haunted verse, and Campos de Castilla, the sterner poems of his Soria years.

In the Castilian poems, bare hills, rivers, and old towns carry thoughts on Spain and loss. His wife Leonor's early death shadows the finest of them. Machado's language is plain, his music quiet, his feeling deep rather than showy. Spain counts him its greatest lyric poet of the twentieth century. This collected edition was the form in which his own age read him whole.
sacconi-summa-de-catharis-1717:
Rainier Sacconi had been a Cathar perfect for seventeen years before he turned Dominican and inquisitor. His Summa de Catharis, written around 1250, reports the sect from the inside. Martène and Durand printed the Latin in their Thesaurus Novus Anecdotorum in 1717. No closer witness to Cathar doctrine survives.

Sacconi maps the Cathar churches of Italy and France, their bishops, their rite of consolamentum, and their split over how the evil world was made. He counts their numbers and names their houses with an ex-member's exactness. His aim was to arm preachers against them, yet his facts outlived his cause. Scholars still start with Sacconi for what the Cathars actually taught.
clarke-leibniz-collection-papers-1717:
Samuel Clarke edited A Collection of Papers in 1717, printing his exchange of letters with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, the great German philosopher. The two men wrote through 1715 and 1716, with Princess Caroline as their go-between, until Leibniz's death ended the contest. An appendix and letters on liberty travel with the main papers.

Space and time stand at the center: are they things in themselves, as Newton and Clarke held, or relations among things, as Leibniz argued? Vacuum, miracles, and God's rule over the world all enter the fight. The Leibniz-Clarke correspondence became the defining debate of early modern metaphysics. It still teaches students how two first-rate minds argue a question to its roots.
millikan-electron-1917:
Robert A. Millikan spent years isolating and measuring the electron, and his 1917 book reports that work. The oil drop experiment sits at its center. By watching tiny charged oil drops hang in an electric field, Millikan fixed the charge of one electron. That number, written as e, became a basic constant of physics.

The book also reports his photoelectric tests of Einstein's equation for light. Those tests backed the idea that light itself comes in quanta. Millikan lays out methods, data, and doubts with unusual care. Readers can follow each step of the measurements. The volume turned hard lab work into settled fact.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol17:
Volume XVII of the Journal of Discourses appeared at Liverpool in 1875, three years before Brigham Young's death. The stenographic record again holds his sermons beside those of his counsellors, the Twelve, and others. A church nearing thirty years in Utah speaks here with the weight of long habit.

Talks in this volume show leaders instructing a people many of whom were born into the faith. Doctrine is less argued than applied, fitted to farms, families, and towns. The year-by-year record gains value from such stretches, where the movement's settled voice can be heard plainly.
russell-finished-mystery-vol7-1917:
The Finished Mystery appeared in 1917, a year after Russell's death, as the seventh Studies in the Scriptures volume. Followers completed it from his notes, expounding Revelation, Ezekiel, and the Song of Solomon verse by verse. The church's leaders hailed it as the founder's posthumous gift to his people.

Instead it split the movement, and its publication fed the great schism of 1918. Governments also seized on its pages during wartime. The volume that was meant to crown the set became its most fought-over book, which makes it key reading on how the Bible Students divided.
twenty-two-goblins-ryder-1917:
Arthur W. Ryder translated Twenty-two Goblins in 1917, from Sivadasa's recension of the Vetala-Panchavimsati. King Vikrama carries a goblin-haunted corpse from a burning ground, and the vetala tells him tales on the road. Each tale ends in a riddle; if the king speaks the answer, the corpse flies back to its tree.

The frame forces the king to repeat his journey again and again, tale after tale. Sanskrit story craft shows at its cleverest here, mixing wit, horror, and moral puzzles. Ryder, a beloved Berkeley teacher, gave the cycle an English as crisp as its own riddles.
lowie-culture-and-ethnology-1917:
Lowie published this slim 1917 volume early in his career, collecting essays that state the Boasian program in miniature. It is a book about how anthropology should be done, written against the loose evolution schemes of the older generation.

The essays take up diffusion, the spread of customs between peoples, and convergence, the separate invention of similar traits. Lowie argues that culture is a patchwork of borrowings, not a ladder of stages. He also defends the culture concept itself as the field's core tool. Short as it is, the book captures the moment American anthropology changed direction.
lawrence-look-we-have-come-through-1917:
Lawrence shaped this 1917 book as a verse sequence: a chain of poems telling one story. It tells of his elopement with Frieda Weekley and their marriage through the war years. Its blunt title announces a survivor's pride.

The poems move from the scandal of their flight to Germany, through poverty and suspicion in wartime England, toward a hard-won sense of arrival. Lawrence called it the essential story of his war years, though no battles appear in it. The fighting here is domestic: love tested by exile, gossip, and want. It remains his most sustained poem sequence, and one of his most personal books.
conrad-shadow-line-1917:
The Shadow-Line, published in 1917, is Conrad's novella of a young captain taking his first command in the East. It is subtitled a confession, and Conrad drew it from his own first command decades before.

The ship is becalmed in the Gulf of Siam, the crew falls sick with fever, and the previous captain's madness seems to haunt the vessel. The narrator must hold his ship and himself together at the border, the shadow line, between youth and maturity. Conrad dedicated it to his son and the young men at war. It is among his most perfect short works.
russell-political-ideals-1917:
Political Ideals, published in 1917, gathers lectures Russell gave while Britain was at war and he was campaigning against it. Excluded from Cambridge for his pacifism, he turned to the question of how political life should be rebuilt after the war.

Russell argues that institutions should be judged by whether they free or stifle creative impulse. He sketches reforms in government, property, and education aimed at growth rather than obedience. The tone is hopeful against the evidence of the trenches. The lectures show Russell the public moralist forming, a role he would play for fifty years.
croce-logic-1917:
Logic as the Science of the Pure Concept, published in English in 1917, is the third volume of Croce's Philosophy of Spirit. It treats thinking proper. This is the theoretical form of spirit that stands beside intuition, its partner and opposite.

Croce argues that the concept is pure when it is universal and concrete at once. He also holds that philosophy and history are the same act of thought seen from two sides. His famous claim for that identity is stated here. The book completes, with the Aesthetic, his account of how the mind knows. It is the most technical of his major works.
plos-pone-0003417:
Delia Goletti and colleagues tested tuberculosis blood tests across Europe in this 2008 study. Newer tests read interferon-gamma released by immune cells, and they improved detection of hidden TB. The open question was how well they find active disease in daily practice. Many clinics in the TBNET network took part.

The team compared single tests with paired test results. Combining tests changed accuracy in ways clinics need to know. The study measured those trade-offs on real patients, not ideal samples. Its findings guide which test mixes doctors should trust for active TB.
plos-pone-0003517:
Emma R. Andersson and co-authors studied a growth signal in the mouse midbrain in this 2008 paper. Wnt5a is a morphogen, a signal that shapes growing tissue. It works through a pathway that orients cells within a sheet. The ventral midbrain grows the dopamine cells lost in Parkinson's disease.

Wnt5a regulated both the shape of that region and its dopamine cells. Groups known as A9 and A10 developed under its guidance. Knowing how those cells form may aid future cell therapies. Their construction rules come from studies like this one. Parkinson's kills these very cells, so their birth rules draw intense study.
plos-pone-0003617:
Federica Rizzi and co-authors proposed a gene test for prostate cancer in this 2008 paper. Prostate cancer is a major cause of cancer death in Western countries. Catching it early, while curable, is highly desirable. Current screening methods carry real limitations.

The signature aims to guide diagnosis for men at risk. Early prostate tumors can often be cured by surgery or radiation alone.
plos-pone-0003717:

The authors show Anc1 takes part in the postreplication repair pathway in baker's yeast. That pathway lets cells cope with damage left behind after DNA copying. The repair role shows a gene-reading helper also guarding the genome once replication has passed.
plos-pone-0003817:

That surface is the first barrier against immune defenses and the handle by which the bacterium attaches to host cells.

The team analyzed the major saccharides, or sugars, associated with the bacterial surface. They show these sugars contribute to how the bacterium associates with host cells. The sugar coat is thus both shield and handshake in infection, and a possible target for blocking it.
plos-pone-0003917:

Their PLOS ONE article follows genome-wide changes as the switch Olig2 drives cell change. They found the Wnt signal path quiets as cells mature. A gene called Dickkopf-1 rises at the same time. Those shifts mark steps that push stem cells toward nerve cell fates. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004017:
Annika M. Sääf, Maria Tengvall-Linder, Howard Y. Chang, and co-authors profiled gene activity in eczema skin in 2008. Atopic eczema is a common chronic inflammatory skin disorder. Genetic studies had found linked regions but few clear genes. Gene activity in diseased skin itself was little known.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a reciprocal pattern in eczema samples. Inflammatory genes rose while lipid genes fell in the skin. Skin lipids form the barrier that keeps water in and germs out. The paired pattern ties barrier failure to immune flare in one picture. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004117:
Jeffrey M. Ellenbogen, Justin C. Hulbert, Ying Jiang, and co-authors tested sleep's effect on verbal memory in 2009. After learning, the brain processes memories during consolidation. Sleep is one known driver of that post-learning change. Behavioral studies link sleep to stronger episodic recall.

Their PLOS ONE article reports sleep boosts resistance to interference. Words learned before sleep survived later distracting material better. Protection from interference is a distinct benefit from simple strengthening. The finding refines advice on timing study and sleep. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004217:
Julian Finn, Tom Tregenza, and Mark Norman published this field study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dolphins are famous for complex social and foraging behaviour, but direct underwater observations of wild dolphins feeding are rare. At mass spawning gatherings of giant cuttlefish in Australia's Upper Spencer Gulf, the authors watched a wild female dolphin hunt.

They describe the complex prey handling she used to prepare her cuttlefish meal, step by step. Preparing a toxic, ink-filled prey animal safely takes skill. The account is a rare close look at how a dolphin turns a difficult animal into food.
plos-pone-0004317:
Valerie White and colleagues published this malaria pathology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The causes of coma and death in cerebral malaria remain unknown. Malarial retinopathy, damage visible in the retina, has been identified as an important clinical sign for diagnosis and prognosis in this disease.

As part of a larger autopsy study of children in Malawi who died in coma, the team examined the retinal pathology of pediatric cerebral malaria. The eye offers a window on the brain's small vessels. What the retina shows at death can test ideas about what kills these children.
plos-pone-0004417: In 2009, Young, Martel, and Young declared tiny nanobacteria dead. The so-called nanobacteria proved to be calcium-homeostasis remnants, not life. garland-son-middle-border-1917:
Garland tells his own story in A Son of the Middle Border, printed from work begun in 1898. In a letter up front he says he first dictated the tale in third person. He calls it his story and the story of his people, the Garlands and the McClintocks.

Boyhood in Wisconsin, Iowa, and Dakota Territory unfolds as his family chased the farming frontier west. Log cabin and prairie claim frame a vivid, novel-like memoir. Garland meant the family record to stand for the whole era of settlement from 1840 to 1914. Issued in 1917, the book is both a personal history and a chronicle of the pioneer generation.
dannunzio-tales-native-town-1917:
Tales of My Native Town gathers D'Annunzio's early stories in a 1917 English edition. The native town lies in the Abruzzo of his boyhood. Peasants, fishermen, priests, and shepherds crowd the brief tales.

These folk live close to the earth and to old folk beliefs. Sights, sounds, and smells of the region soak every page. The great decadent of later fame is not yet on show here. A young writer drunk on his home ground writes instead, fresh and direct. For new readers, these tales rank among his easiest and most winning works, a clean start before the fevered novels.
maier-silentium-post-clamores-1617:
Michael Maier answers the Rosicrucian uproar in Silentium Post Clamores, in Latin from 1617: silence after the outcry. The emperor's physician defends the unknown brotherhood with deep learning. Alchemy, music, and the hidden arts fill his eloquent plea for the Rosy Cross and its promised reform of all human knowledge.

Maier asks why the brethren keep silent amid such clamor. His answer weaves wisdom literature with courtly tact and hope. The book opens a window on the dreams of 1617 in Europe. It stands as the most eloquent defense the Rosicrucians ever received, from a man whose own alchemical works remain classics of their kind.
reuchlin-de-arte-cabalistica-1517:
Johann Reuchlin founds Christian Kabbalah in De Arte Cabalistica, in Latin from 1517. The great humanist teaches Christians to read the Jewish mystics with respect. Hebrew letters hide, in his account, deep truths about God and Christ that Greek and Latin learning alone could never have found without the key.

Reuchlin risked his name to defend Jewish books from the flames. His stand made him the hero of the humanists' war against obscurantism. Erasmus and his circle rallied to the aging scholar's cause in print. The book brought Kabbalah into Renaissance thought for good, and it still marks the spot where two great traditions met in one mind.
whiston-astronomical-principles-religion:
William Whiston held Newton's chair at Cambridge and wrote on both science and faith. His Astronomical Principles of Religion came out in 1717. In it he read the Bible through the lens of the new astronomy of his day.

Whiston argued that a comet passing near Earth had caused the great Flood. He linked planets, comets, and scripture into one bold system of causes. The book mixes real skill in astronomy with deep trust in revealed truth. It shows an early clash, and an early truce, between Newton's cosmos and the Bible that shaped his age.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-17:
Westward push and fresh danger shape Volume 17, issued in 1898. Thwaites covers the Hurons and Three Rivers across 1639 and 1640. At peak trust, the mission reaches toward new nations in the west.

Black robes carry the cross deeper into the continent each season. Their letters weigh new tongues, new trails, and new allies with care. Far off, the Iroquois wars begin to close around them. Growth and threat fill the same pages in tense balance. The volume catches the mission at full stretch, just before the noose tightens around it. Ambition and peril grow side by side here.
journal-of-discourses-vol-17:
Young's seventieth year lends Volume Seventeen, from 1875, a backward gaze. The prophet surveys the kingdom he built across the Great Basin. Desert made to blossom stands as his life's plain, visible proof.

Discourses recall the exodus, the first camps, and the gathered Saints. An old leader counts his works as the succession draws near. Pride and warning mix in his late, summing voice from the stand. The flock hears a founder bless and brace them in one breath. Few volumes in the set feel so much like a testament before the end comes. Age lends his counsel a weight no younger voice could match.
zimmermann-telegram-1917:
Arthur Zimmermann, Germany's foreign chief, sent his famed telegram in 1917. The secret offer invites Mexico to join a war on America. Texas and the Southwest are dangled as the prize for joining.

British codebreakers seize the message and pass it to Washington with care. American papers print it, and public fury sweeps the neutral nation. Within weeks, the United States declares war on Germany at last. One intercepted cable thus swings the whole Great War's balance. Few single messages in history have changed so much so fast for so many. Germany's bid for a second front collapsed the moment it leaked.
simmel-grundfragen-der-soziologie-1917:
Georg Simmel published his Fundamental Questions of Sociology in German in 1917, late in a career spent mostly outside the university's inner circle. Sociology was still a young science without a settled subject. Simmel's little book asks what that subject really is, and answers with the clarity of a lifetime's thought.

His answer: sociology studies the forms of human association, the patterns by which people join, rule, compete, and cooperate. The same forms, the dyad, the triad, the stranger, recur in churches, armies, and markets alike. Content changes; the geometry of relations endures. The book is the Berlin master's late, brief statement of his life's theme. It remains the clearest short door into Simmel's work, the place where society's geometry is traced in a few bold lines.

Method papers mattered because photo judgments carried real weight for missing men's files. A loose standard could raise false hope or bury a true match. Here the analysts set out careful rules for their own craft. Historians of the POW effort value such texts for showing the science behind the casework. The paper takes the measure of that fight closely. It weighs the rebels' craft against the police and army hunting them. For readers, it is an early study of a new kind of war.
