plos-pone-0005417: The Baltic Sea chokes on excess phosphorus. Bryhn used a dynamic mass-balance model to identify sustainable phosphorus loadings and cost-effective management. The modeling guides policy for clearer waters. Saving a sea with smarter nutrient budgets, country by country, four decades of algal blooms demand exactly this analysis.
plos-pone-0005517: Gut Escherichia coli may promote colon cancer by crippling DNA repair. Maddocks and team showed attaching and effacing Escherichia coli downregulate mismatch-repair proteins and associate with human adenocarcinomas. The germ link to tumor growth strengthens. Germs undermining genomic guardians in the human colon.
plos-pone-0005617: TB kills two million yearly, and new drugs are urgent. Al-Balas and team found aminothiazole derivatives active against Mycobacterium tuberculosis and its FabH enzyme. The compounds hit a validated target. New reactions against an old killer, designed for drug defense.
plos-pone-0005717: NRAS-mutant tumors resist single-pathway drugs. Jaiswal and team showed combined BRAF/CRAF or BRAF/PI3K targeting works in NRAS tumors. The combination plan defeats defense. Hitting cancer's backup pathways, two at once, RAS-effector inhibition tailored to mutation, in combination therapy for a tough oncogene.
plos-pone-0005817: Heart attack clots hold clues about plaque rupture. Kramer and team laid out sucked out thrombi from STEMI patients after PCI. The tissue study times plaque break. Clots telling cardiac stories, under the lens, acute heart syndromes' process, break and block split in time.
plos-pone-0006417: Lab-grown beta cells drift off course. Russ and team found human beta cells shift toward a new form when grown in dishes. The drift blocks high-sugar illness therapy — beta cells lose themselves, traced, from adult islets as source, with lineage tracking used.
plos-pone-0006517: A slow virus packs T cells with trouble. Yamano and team found HTLV-1-infected T cells stacked with swelling markers in HAM/TSP. The loaded cells drive nerve ills — infected cells' fingerprint, mapped, in chronic nerve ills. ATL link, disease path probed: high levels found.
plos-pone-0006617: Identical twins, different Alzheimer's fate. Mastroeni and team found tag-based gaps in neurons of twins split by Alzheimer's. The tags tell the tale — same genes, different destiny, mapped, via DNA tagging. Brain-surface neurons, rare pair: pathways tuned, look's roots, split decoded.
plos-pone-0009417: The placenta forms when certain cells fuse into one giant layer, a process whose failure underlies miscarriage and preeclampsia. Tracking human placental cells in the dish, the authors found a master switch, the protein NR2F2, surging nearly nine-fold as fusion begins. The paper identifies a key controller of the placenta's formation — and a new suspect when pregnancies go wrong early.
plos-pone-0009517: Why are some animal groups wildly diverse in skull shape while others stay uniform? This study tests whether modularity — the skull being built from semi-independent parts — lets carnivores and primates evolve more varied faces. The paper links the architecture of development to the spectacular variety of mammalian skulls.
plos-pone-0009617: Do migrants need bigger brains? Comparing songbirds, this study finds migratory species tend to have smaller brains than their stay-at-home cousins. The paper adds a surprising twist to brain evolution: the demands of migration may favor leaner minds.
plos-pone-0010417: Aphids without soldier castes or ant bodyguards still fight back — together. This study documents collective defense in two aphid species against predators. The paper shows that even the meekest insects can mount a group defense. The work proves you don't need soldiers or allies to defend a colony — just numbers and nerve.
plos-pone-0010517: Reading complete gene transcripts reveals how genes are spliced. This study presents a cheaper hybrid assembly method for sequencing full-length cDNAs. The paper makes gene-structure mapping more affordable for labs everywhere. Cheaper sequencing puts full gene maps within reach of smaller labs.
plos-pone-0010617: The way a molecule twists light can reveal its 3D shape. This study measures the circular dichroism of new bicolchicide compounds, a fresh pseudoaromatic family. The spectra decode how their light-bending parts interact. The paper shows a classic spectroscopy technique cracking the structure of novel molecules.
plos-pone-0010717: During Toronto's 2003 SARS outbreak, the virus spread inside hospitals. This multicenter study hunted the risk factors for transmission from patients needing intubation. Certain procedures proved riskiest. The paper gives health workers evidence-based protection guidance. The lessons apply to future respiratory outbreaks.
plos-pone-0010817: Chronic fatigue syndrome still lacks a lab test. This study evaluates natural killer cell function and the DPP-IV/CD26 marker as candidate biomarkers. The paper puts numbers on immune differences. The findings move diagnosis beyond symptoms alone. The markers could validate patients' suffering.
plos-pone-0010917: Endothelin-1 clamps blood vessels shut — hard to reverse. This study shows stimulating sensory-motor nerves breaks the ET-1 receptor's grip via CGRP release. The paper reveals a neural off-switch. The finding informs cardiovascular medicine. The off-switch could inspire new blood-pressure drugs.
plos-pone-0011017: Healing proteins vanish from the blood in minutes. This study traps growth factors in a self-assembled polycation-heparin complex for controlled release. The paper delivers a drug-delivery depot. The system could make growth-factor therapy practical. The depot releases healing proteins on a slow schedule.
plos-pone-0011117: Some cattle resist Johne's disease better than others. This study hunts the genetic loci behind antibody responses to Mycobacterium avium paratuberculosis in cattle. The paper maps resistance genes. The finding could guide selective breeding. The breeding could cut livestock losses.
plos-pone-0011217: Dying worm cells shred their DNA into a ladder pattern. This study shows the small DNA pieces in C. elegans are intermediates of apoptotic DNA fragmentation. The paper confirms a cell-death hallmark. The finding aids apoptosis research. The hallmark validates worm death models.
plos-pone-0011317: Elderly flu deaths depend on vaccine match. This Taiwan study evaluates how matching vaccine strains and post-SARS public health efforts reduced influenza-associated mortality among the elderly. The paper offers a public-health model. The finding informs vaccination policy. The informed policy saves elderly lives.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1217:
Vincent, chief of the Division of Chinese Affairs, wrote to Assistant Secretary Dunn on 23 July 1945. Vincent's desk owned the China file inside the State Department. His note moved expert judgment up to a senior chief while the summit sat.

China questions at Potsdam touched Soviet pledges in Asia and America's hopes for a stable ally. The desk chief's view fed the stands the team took. A note of this kind is the expert layer speaking in its own channel. It shows the department's China knowledge being put at the service of men deciding far larger questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1317:
Pauley, the American member of the Allied Commission on Reparations, wrote to the President on 19 July 1945. Edwin Pauley's mission had toured beaten Germany to judge what the nation could pay and what could be taken in goods, plants, and labor.

Reparations were among the sharpest fights at Potsdam. The Soviet side claimed vast sums; the Americans feared a repeat of the debts that poisoned the last peace. Pauley's reports gave the president the facts from the ground. This message is his word to the top, feeding the summit's hardest money bargain with first-hand evidence.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1417:
The communiqué issued at the end of the Yalta Conference in February 1945 is reprinted in the Potsdam volume. It was the public statement of what Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin had agreed in the Crimea. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A communiqué speaks to the world, so its tone is proud and its edges smooth. Read beside the Yalta protocol, also reprinted here, it shows the gap between what the leaders announced and what they had in fact signed. The Potsdam editors placed both Yalta texts at the back of their volume as a bench mark. Readers can measure the distance traveled between February and August 1945 in these pages.
frus-1945-50-intel-d17:
Attorney General Tom Clark wrote to President Truman on 19 September 1945, the day before the OSS was dissolved. Clark's department housed the FBI, whose director reported to him. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The attorney general's voice mattered in the intelligence fight because the FBI's foreign work hung in the balance. Clark wrote as the president's choice neared, putting the Justice Department's case at the top level. Readers can set his letter beside Hoover's papers to Clark from the same weeks. Together they show a department aligning its front. The bureau chief pressed his chief, and the chief pressed the president, in the last hours before the order fell.
frus-1945-50-intel-d117:
Acting Secretary Acheson sent a memorandum to the members of the National Intelligence Authority on 5 August 1946. The authority was the board of secretaries that owned the Central Intelligence Group. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A memorandum to the whole authority put a question before every member at once, in identical words. By August the FBI and CIG fight over Latin America needed the board's ruling, and Acheson's paper belongs to that endgame. Readers should watch how the system handled its first great internal dispute. Not by a president's order, but by the board the January directive had built for the purpose. The machinery, tested here, either worked or showed its cracks.
frus-1945-50-intel-d217:
The Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) addressed a letter to the Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee (Gurney) on 3 June 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 217 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. That season, the talk in Washington was of one big law to join up defense, foreign policy, and intelligence.

The letter form mattered in this world: it was signed, it was kept, and it bound the writer's office to what it said. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. The letter went to the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee while Congress debated the law that created the CIA.
frus-1945-50-intel-d317:
Dated 13 May 1947, "Central Intelligence Group Paper No. 24/1" comes from the top level of the government. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 317 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Papers of this kind were the working stock of the system. They were drafted, read, marked up, and filed so the next office could pick up the thread. Read with its neighbors, it helps fill the gaps that grand accounts skip over. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d417:
A memo dated 23 February 1950 was prepared for James Lay, executive secretary of the National Security Council. It is document 417 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Lay's office set the Council's agenda and moved its papers to the President. A memo addressed to him was aimed at the center of the policy machine. Readers meet the staff layer that turned the views of departments into choices laid before Harry Truman. A memo for Lay was, in effect, a memo for the President's desk by a longer road.
frus-1861-d17:
Norman Judd wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 27 August 1861. The dispatch is document 17 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Judd's post in Berlin gave him a view of German opinion as the war dragged on. He reported what he saw and heard for a Secretary who read every such line with care. The letter forms one link in a chain of reports that ran from Berlin to Washington all through 1861. The Berlin file is modest in size, yet it runs the full span of the year's record.
frus-1861-d117:
John Lothrop Motley, bound for Vienna as minister to Austria, received a letter from William H. Seward on 27 August 1861. Motley was the new American minister to Austria, bound for Vienna. The letter is document 117 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Motley was a famed historian of the Dutch republic before he was an envoy. Seward sent him to a court that prized rank and form. The August letter belongs to the start of Motley's term, as he learned the trade of diplomacy at Vienna. Motley's histories of the Dutch wars against Spain still sat on scholars' shelves in 1861.
frus-1861-d217:
A State Department letter of 23 July 1861 told Mr. Marsh what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 217 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d17:
A dispatch dated 13 February 1862 carried word from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 17 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d117:
A dispatch dated 1 August 1862 carried word from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 117 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d217:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, opened a new run of letters on 20 June 1862, writing to Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington. The letter is Document 217 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William Stuart was acting head of the legation while Lord Lyons was away.

With Lyons absent, Stuart handled Britain's American business through a hard summer. Seward dealt with him as he had with Lyons, by frequent short letters. The Stuart file that follows covers months when Union arms faltered in Virginia and European talk of stepping into the war grew louder. The British legation stood a short walk from the State Department, and messengers passed between them daily.
frus-1862-d317:
Document 317 completes the four Seward dispatches to Paris dated 24 September 1862 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The set went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Four letters in a day also hint at the steamer schedule: when a ship sailed, the bag had to be ready. The set sailed into an Atlantic of changed politics, since emancipation was now Union policy. Read together, Documents 314 through 317 give the fullest single-day picture of Washington's Paris brief in the whole 1862 file. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d417:
Writing from Madrid on 30 March 1862, Horace J. Perry sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 417 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

End of March 1862 found Spain pulling back from the joint Mexican venture as French aims there grew plain, a split Washington welcomed. Perry's post let him report that shift from inside the Spanish capital. His letters home formed one strand of the record by which the Union tracked Europe's mood. It did so port by port and court by court, while its armies fought to restore the nation.
frus-1862-d517:
On 6 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. The instruction is Document 517 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Seward wrote with Lee's army on Union soil and the government bracing for the Maryland campaign. His September orders to Europe's posts struck one note: confidence, and no welcome for foreign interference whatever came. At The Hague that note fell on friendly ears. Pike's long file with Seward shows two plain-spoken men keeping a minor post in exact step with a major policy. The dispatch belongs to the tense fortnight in which the Union's fate, at home and abroad, hung on one campaign.
frus-1862-d617:
On 22 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to Bradford R. Wood. It is Document 617 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Late April 1862 was the spring's most hopeful moment in Washington, with New Orleans about to fall. Orders to friendly minor courts in those weeks spread the improving story and kept routine business current. Wood's Denmark file shows how the Department maintained its whole network at once. No post was too small for a monthly letter. No minister was left to guess at the government's line. The instruction is a modest piece of that maintenance, valuable to the reader chiefly as part of the complete pattern.
frus-1862-d717:
Luis Molina wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 October 1862. He was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington. The letter is document 717 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, late in the two men's fall exchange.

By October the Molina file had grown into one of the busier small files in the volume. His letters kept Costa Rica's questions in front of the State Department, and Seward's answers kept the tie in good repair. This letter is a late piece of that work. It shows a small land's envoy doing his job with care in a capital gripped by war.
frus-1863p1-d17:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 20 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London, and the letter is document 17 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward wrote in the last days of a hard year.

The year 1862 had brought the Union near ruin more than once, and Britain's stance still hung in the scale. Seward's letters to London pressed the same claims with fresh force as news changed. This one belongs to the year-end run, when Washington took stock and told its envoy how to open the new year. It is desk work of the highest stakes.
frus-1863p1-d117:
On 13 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 117 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of a pair often bore the fuller tale: a talk writ large, a set of facts laid out. Adams wrote so through the spring of 1863. This letter is the mate to document 116. In the run of the file, the pair shows a post sorting a mass of news into clean parts. They were bound for a reader ten days away by sea.
frus-1863p1-d217:
An instruction dated 18 June 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 217 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d317:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 November 1862. His note is document 317 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Small cases fill this part of the volume: a vessel, a cargo, a British subject under arrest. Together they show how a war at sea kept landing on diplomats' desks. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d417:
A note dated 17 March 1863 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 417 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d517:
Among the day's business on 18 May 1863 was a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d617:
Document 617 in the volume is a letter of 12 September 1863 from William H. Seward to William Stuart. Stuart was Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020217:
Anke Steppuhn, Klaus Gase, Bernd Krock, and their team tested nicotine's role in wild tobacco plants for PLOS Biology in 2004. Nicotine is a poison the plant makes in its leaves. The team lowered nicotine in plants growing in nature and watched what insects did.

With less nicotine, more leaf-eating insects fed on the plants, and damage rose. That is direct field proof that nicotine defends the plant, not just a lab guess. The study also weighed costs, since making poison takes energy the plant could spend on growth or seeds. Field tests like this one ground chemical ecology in real conditions, where weather, rivals, and many insect species all play a part.
plos-pone-0000117:
Pertti Happonen, Sari Voutilainen, Tomi-Pekka Tuomainen, and colleagues published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It asks whether a common gene variant changes how coffee drinking affects the risk of a sudden coronary event, such as a heart attack. The gene makes an enzyme called COMT, which breaks down stress hormones.

Coffee has been blamed and praised for heart risk for decades, with mixed study results. The authors test whether a person's version of this gene tips the balance of coffee's effect. If genes change who is harmed or helped by coffee, broad advice to all drinkers may need to become more personal.
plos-pone-0000217:
Olivier Tenaillon, Olin K. Silander, Jean-Philippe Uzan, and colleagues published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks how to put a number on complexity, how complex a living thing is, using the tools of population genetics. Instead of counting body parts, the authors ground complexity in the genetics of populations.

Complexity is easy to sense and hard to measure. Their definition ties it to mutation, selection, and drift, things that can be counted and measured. The paper offers a yardstick for comparing organisms from bacteria to mammals, and for testing claims about whether evolution tends toward greater complexity.
plos-pone-0000317:
Hiroaki Murakami, Derek B. Goto, Takashi Toda, and colleagues published this cell division paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dis3 is a ribonuclease, an enzyme that chews up RNA. The authors show its activity is required for mitotic progression, the orderly march through cell division. It also links heterochromatin, densely packed DNA, to the kinetochore, the handle by which chromosomes are pulled apart.

A defective Dis3 stalls division and disturbs chromosome handling. Connecting an RNA-chewing enzyme to chromosome segregation was unexpected, and it is the kind of link few had looked for. The finding helps explain how cells keep their silent DNA regions and their division machinery working together.
plos-pone-0000417:
Yoshiyasu Arai and colleagues located where each beat of spinal rhythm begins in the chick embryo, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Even before birth, the spinal cord can generate rhythmic activity, the patterning behind stepping and swimming. The team asked which side region of the cord starts each cycle.

Their title gives the answer they found: each cycle arises from the ventrolateral region of the cord. Knowing where a rhythm starts helps map the circuits that produce it. Chick embryos are a classic system for this work. Their spinal circuits can be studied while still developing. That helps explain how locomotion circuits are built.
plos-pone-0000517:
Ewan P. Plant and colleagues studied how the ribosome reads near-miss instructions, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The ribosome builds proteins by reading codons, three-letter words in the genetic message. Near-cognate codons differ by one letter from the correct word. They should be rejected. Working in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the team studied how the cell tells near- from non-cognate codons.

Reading errors produce faulty proteins, so the ribosome proofreads, but not perfectly. Understanding the discrimination steps explains the accuracy of all protein production and how antibiotics that jam the ribosome exploit its weak points. Yeast is the standard test bed for this universal machinery.
plos-pone-0000617:
Alex S. Nord, Karen Vranizan, Whittemore Tingley and colleagues built a model of gene trapping for PLOS ONE in 2007. Gene trapping inserts new DNA into mouse embryonic stem cells to disrupt genes and reveal what they do. It is the most widely used form of insertional mutagenesis in mammals. Yet the rules that govern how well it works were not fully known.

Their model uses two features of each gene: its length and how strongly it is expressed. A good model would let labs predict which genes a trap will hit and which it will miss. That matters for large projects that map gene function across the whole mammalian genome.
plos-pone-0000717:
Hervé Philippe, Henner Brinkmann, Pedro Martinez and colleagues argued that acoel flatworms do not belong where textbooks put them. Acoels are small marine worms traditionally classed in the phylum Platyhelminthes, the flatworms. Molecular phylogenetic analyses suggest instead that acoels are surviving members of the earliest diverging Bilateria, the great animal group with left-right symmetry.

Their evidence comes from phylogenomics, family trees built from many genes at once. Moving acoels to the base of the bilaterian tree changes what scientists infer about the first bilaterians. Traits acoels lack might be later inventions rather than losses. Few classification fights carry stakes that deep in animal history.
plos-pone-0000817:
Dorit Ben-Shachar and Rachel Karry linked a general gene switch to energy genes behaving oddly in schizophrenia, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The prevailing hypothesis treats schizophrenia as a polygenic disease, where many genes combine with each other and with environmental stimuli to produce its varied symptoms. The authors investigated whether the ubiquitous transcription factor Sp1 is abnormally expressed in the disease.

Their title states the chain they propose: Sp1 expression is disrupted in schizophrenia. That disruption offers a possible mechanism for the abnormal expression of mitochondrial complex I genes NDUFV1 and NDUFV2. One faulty master switch could explain several downstream faults at once, an appealing pattern in a complex disease.
plos-pone-0000917:
Ziming Weng, Roger Barthelson, Siddarame Gowda and colleagues showed how mixed virus infections inside one host breed diversity, in PLOS ONE in 2007. When viral genomes recombine or swap segments, new viruses can emerge. Long lasting infections raise the odds, because several genotypes can copy themselves side by side in a single host.

The team followed an RNA virus held in persistent infection. With multiple genotypes present, recombination ran freely and produced wide variety. That variety is raw material for new viral forms. The study explains one route by which plant and animal viruses keep changing under our feet.
plos-pone-0001017:
William Laurance, Henrique Nascimento, Susan Laurance and colleagues measured how uneven forest edge effects can be, in PLOS ONE in 2007. When forest is cut into fragments, the edges change: light, wind and invading species press in. Those edge effects drive much of what happens next, yet they vary greatly in space and time.

The team assessed that variability across Amazon forest dynamics, plant makeup, invading species and carbon storage. Their landscape divergence idea holds that fragments do not all follow one path. Management based on a single average edge could mislead badly. The study argues for reading each fragment's own trajectory.
plos-pone-0001117:
Shai Shaham's 2007 PLOS ONE article deals with a practical question in genetics: how many altered genomes has a screen actually checked? Genetic screens in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans can mean examining thousands or tens of thousands of animals, each carrying scrambled DNA.

Shaham lays out how to count the mutagenized gametes a screen has covered. That count shapes how researchers judge a screen's progress. It also helps them guess how many genes can produce a given trait, and weigh the cost of going further. The paper gives worm geneticists a clearer way to plan screens and to know when one has run long enough.
plos-pone-0001217:
TOR is a protein kinase, a master switch for cell growth found in nearly all complex life. Kathrin Thedieck and colleagues identified new partners of the mammalian version, mTOR, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. mTOR sits in two distinct complexes, TORC1 and TORC2, with different jobs.

The authors report that two proteins, PRAS40 and a PRR5-like protein, are new mTOR interactors that regulate apoptosis, programmed cell death. Adding members to the mTOR complexes refines the wiring diagram of growth control. Because mTOR is a major cancer drug target, its full cast of partners matters.
plos-pone-0001317:
Serotonin receptors of the 5-HT4 type are drug targets for gut and brain disorders. Wei Chun Chang and colleagues studied how this receptor signals, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. G protein-coupled receptors like 5-HT4 signal through a limited number of pathways. They play crucial roles in many processes, but their diversity makes in vivo study hard.

The authors address modifying ligand-induced and constitutive signaling of the human 5-HT4 receptor. Constitutive signaling means the receptor is partly active even with no serotonin present. Tools that tune each mode separately would help both research and drug design.
plos-pone-0001417:
Petr Ilyinskii and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a flu protein that harms the cells that make it. Shots built on this protein, called M2, had shown mixed success in past tests. The team had found that M2 kills host cells grown in the lab. They asked whether curbing that harm could make shots work better.

The authors report that blocking M2 driven cell death lifts its drag on shot strength. In other words, the protein was hurting its own use as a vaccine base. Fixing that flaw could revive a shot idea with broad appeal. A flu shot that works across strains stays a top goal.
plos-pone-0001517:
Alexander Chesler and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on switching genes in smell nerve cells. New smell neurons are born through life, but how they wire in was a mystery. The team built a way to add genes to young smell neurons in live mice. The method uses a mild electric pulse after birth.
